note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Trace ONE complete mature flowering culm: Florida paspalum usually bears about 2–5 one-sided racemes attached at different points along the axis. Existing species gallery panels 1 and 2 show actual attached flowering racemes and rounded spikelets from David J. Stang's source-labelled cultivated plant; panel 0 shows the broader bunch habit. The two Stang JPEG archives were independently checked for byte integrity, dimensions and source rights on October 26, but neither is a Hays County voucher or supplies a millimeter scale. Do not infer measured spikelet size, local occurrence, or rooted rhizome anatomy from those pictures.
tiles.short: Few long racemes with broad paired 'coins'
tiles.status: GROSS FIELD CUE VISIBLE; SAME-PLANT ROOT-TO-HEAD PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK THE RHIZOME AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: A robust perennial with short rhizomes. Open the INNER blade/sheath junction to expose the true membranous ligule: Williamson County treatment gives approximately 1.5–2.5 mm, while USGS describes about 1.2–3.3 mm. Nearby collar/sheath hairs are separate. Panel 5 shows a DALLISGRASS collar (different species) for location only, NOT evidence of Florida paspalum's ligule.
tiles.short: Short stout rhizomes; real membrane, not hairs
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — ROOTED CROWN AND MEASURED TRUE MEMBRANE

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE PAIRED MATURE SPIKELETS
tiles.details: On one unilateral raceme, find adjacent paired dorsally compressed oval spikelets. Existing species gallery panels 1–2 actually show rounded attached spikelets and raceme attachment, including gross-organ arrows, but NO scale or opened florets. UT Williamson County treatment reports mature spikelets about 3.5–4.2 × 2.8–3.2 mm; photograph several ripe pairs flat-face and edge-on with a 1-mm scale before claiming a measured distinction from hairyseed paspalum.
tiles.status: ACTUAL ATTACHED SPIKELETS VISIBLE — MEASURED MATURE PAIRS AND DISSECTION NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · SEPARATE GLUME, LEMMAS AND PALEA
tiles.details: A true LOWER GLUME is absent. The upper glume is approximately 3.5–4 mm and five-veined; the lower sterile lemma is roughly its length, while the hard upper fertile lemma is about 3 × 2.6 mm and encloses a palea. There are no long projecting awns. Do not label the adjacent PAIR of spikelets as two florets, or invent a missing lower glume. These parts require a ripe dissection.
tiles.short: No lower glume; upper glume ~3.5–4 mm

tiles.heading: 05 · SEPARATE LOCAL PASPALUM LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Panel 3 is DALLISGRASS (P. dilatatum), not Florida paspalum: compare its long silky upper-glume hairs and typically more numerous narrower spikelets. Panel 4 is HAIRYSEED PASPALUM (P. pubiflorum), often with smaller ~2.7–3.2 mm mature spikelets. Vaseygrass (P. urvillei) often has many more racemes and smaller spikelets. Branch counts and spikelet sizes overlap; use actual measured same-maturity anatomy.
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE PHOTOS LABELLED; MATCHED MATURE MACROS MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · REQUIRE PHOTO AND SITE PROOF
tiles.details: Before marking FINISHED, obtain a voucher-confirmed local plant linking crown, true 1–3 mm membranous ligule, full head and 3.5–4.2 mm paired mature spikelets. Dissect upper glume, sterile lemma, hard fertile lemma and palea under a calibrated macro. Check public reuse for each archived JPEG and every arrow against actual visible pixels; existing comparison photos must remain correctly labelled. Preserve taxonomy and nativity holds.
tiles.short: One rooted plant, collar and dissected spikelet

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FLORIDA PASPALUM — trace a robust leafy stem to its COMPLETE terminal head, often 2–5 long spikelet-bearing racemes attached at different points. On each one-sided raceme look for large, smooth, fairly rounded flattened paired 'coins'; measure actual mature spikelets (~3.5–4.2 mm in the UT Texas treatment) against a 1-mm scale. For sterile plants check the ACTUAL 1.2–3.3 mm brown membranous ligule at the blade–sheath junction and short stout rhizomatous crown, unlike switchgrass's hair-fringe ligule and Indiangrass's claw/auricled collar. No current target-species photo proves the membrane or separate glumes; keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: LOOK at actual Florida paspalum habit (gallery image 0). This source-reported clump image is real but not diagnostic without the head.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: A robust perennial with short rhizomes. Open the INNER blade/sheath junction to expose the true membranous ligule: Williamson County treatment gives approximately 1.5–2.5 mm, while USGS describes about 1.2–3.3 mm. Nearby collar/sheath hairs are separate. Panel 5 shows a DALLISGRASS collar (different species) for location only, NOT evidence of Florida paspalum's ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: On one unilateral raceme, find adjacent paired dorsally compressed oval spikelets. Existing species gallery panels 1–2 actually show rounded attached spikelets and raceme attachment, including gross-organ arrows, but NO scale or opened florets. UT Williamson County treatment reports mature spikelets about 3.5–4.2 × 2.8–3.2 mm; photograph several ripe pairs flat-face and edge-on with a 1-mm scale before claiming a measured distinction from hairyseed paspalum.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Compare Florida paspalum's broad large roundish spikelets and few racemes against smaller 2.7–3.2 mm P. pubiflorum. Both can have multiple racemes; don't conclude species from grass size or a garden photograph. Dallisgrass should have distinctive long marginal spikelet hairs.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: FLORIDA PASPALUM — trace a robust leafy stem to its COMPLETE terminal head, often 2–5 long spikelet-bearing racemes attached at different points. On each one-sided raceme look for large, smooth, fairly rounded flattened paired 'coins'; measure actual mature spikelets (~3.5–4.2 mm in the UT Texas treatment) against a 1-mm scale. For sterile plants check the ACTUAL 1.2–3.3 mm brown membranous ligule at the blade–sheath junction and short stout rhizomatous crown, unlike switchgrass's hair-fringe ligule and Indiangrass's claw/auricled collar. No current target-species photo proves the membrane or separate glumes; keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
memory_rule: COUNT THE WHOLE RACEMES (usually 2–5), inspect paired large coin-shaped spikelets along one side, then photograph the TRUE brown membranous ligule. P. pubiflorum has smaller similar units; no single unscaled photograph certifies the species.
safety_note: Gross photo structures are references, NOT expert confirmation. Even new licensed images are PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING and not proof of Hays County presence.
field_rule: Florida paspalum tends to have big coarse basal clumps with relatively few long racemes and large often rounded spikelets. Dallisgrass generally has conspicuous long silky hairs fringing its large spikelets; vaseygrass often has much more numerous finer racemes with smaller spikelets. P. pubiflorum commonly has smaller 2.7–3.2 mm spikelets, and pubescence needs careful comparison.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Compare Florida paspalum's broad large roundish spikelets and few racemes against smaller 2.7–3.2 mm P. pubiflorum. Both can have multiple racemes; don't conclude species from grass size or a garden photograph. Dallisgrass should have distinctive long marginal spikelet hairs.
